utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Please be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, Sureta Chana, Julian Nicholls, for the Prosecution, assisted by case manager Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. And good morning to you all. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Cunningham with John Ackerman and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you all. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: A couple of things, Your Honour. In going through our database, we found that this case had given us a statement. I have made copies and provided it to the Chamber. That statement as soon as I found it in our database, I emailed it to the Prosecution. And it just merely discusses his role in the arrest of the Mice. There's a logistical matter I'd like to get the Chamber's feedback. We have put all the English exhibits that we intend to use today on Sanction. What we propose to do is to have a binder that already has the Serbian exhibits pulled, tabbed, and we could direct him to that if that's okay with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's okay with the Prosecution, it's okay with the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: They indicated they had no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we will proceed. The important thing, I would like to have those documents put on the ELMO at least for a while because I want to see what's highlighted and what's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: There are two documents that are highlighted, and basically it's -- and I'll alert the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And Mr. Ackerman will have them on Sanction and have the relevant parts highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say something here? We did receive these -- the statement yesterday, which was Sunday, including the exhibit list. I just want the record to reflect that we got it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Before we bring in the witness, Madam Registrar, can you just follow me, we are sitting this week through Thursday, stopping Friday?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To give the Defence a chance to go on site as requested. 25th of November which was a sitting day is now a holiday. The Eid Al-Fitr holiday. Okay. 26th we're not scheduled to sit, but we will be sitting.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, that week, 26, 27, 28, correct me if I am wrong, Madam Registrar, we are sitting in the morning in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the first week in December, Monday 1st December right through Friday, 5th December. Which courtroom will we be sitting and what time?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We will be sitting Courtroom I from 2.15 to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you have in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: At the moment nothing scheduled in Courtroom I in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Because the list that I had showed Dragan Nikolic by mistake there putting us in the afternoon because of that case. Now that case is over. The sentencing hearing was finished last week, so whoever put that there in that week made a mistake. So if you could transfer all the afternoon sittings to the morning, right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't hear you, because I have this and you have the microphone switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Perhaps we have to compromise in the sense that sometimes in the morning Milosevic will be sitting in Courtroom I, and another case will be in the morning too. Then we have to switch from courtroom to courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, that's not a problem. The important thing is that we sit in the morning rather than in the afternoon. So I leave this matter in your hands. And while we proceed with the witness, perhaps you can find out exactly -- the same applies to the following week, until the 19th. Check whether there are any days when we are scheduled to sit in the afternoon. And see if we could have them transferred to the morning. Keep in mind also that on the 2nd of December, probably Hadzihasanovic trial will start. So we'll have to find -- make sure that we don't clash with that. All right? Thanks. Let's bring the witness in, please. Madam usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Savic, and welcome to this Tribunal. You are going to give evidence, and before you do so our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration, that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. It's the equivalent of an oath. Please proceed. Read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please be seated. You know you have been summoned to give evidence by Mr. Brdjanin, who's the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which basically means that you are going to be asked a series of questions first by his lawyer. In this case, it's going to be Mr. Cunningham, the gentleman in the front row in the middle. He will then be followed by the Prosecution, and Madam -- I take it you will be cross-examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will be cross-examining you. The fact that you are a Defence witness does not entitle you to draw any distinction or make any distinction between questions coming from the Defence or questions coming from the Prosecution. The reason -- the purpose for taking the oath, for making that solemn declaration, is, in fact, the need and consequently the obligation on your part to answer each question as fully and as truthfully as possible, irrespective of who is putting the question to you. Did I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Cunningham, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Cunningham:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your name is Milenko Savic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which municipality do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I currently reside in Prnjavor Municipality. I was born in Hrvacani near Prijedor. Am I supposed to say anything else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'd like for you to do is just listen to the question, and answer only the question. Don't volunteer any additional information. If myself or the Prosecutor or the Chamber needs additional information from you, they'll let you know. You were born in Prnjavor Municipality. Which municipality do you currently work in?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your position there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I am an inspector for white-collar crime in the public security station of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long have you been involved in law enforcement, been a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I've worked since the 1st of April, 1990, that is for over 13 years I worked as a policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like for you to tell the Chamber about your educational experience. Did you attend secondary school?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I graduated from the school of economics in Banja Luka. Then I obtained the associate degree in economics and eventually I got a full university degree in economics from the University of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you acquire your degree from Banja Luka University? What year?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I graduated in 1980, and I obtained the associate degree in economics in 1974.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were attending university, were you a full-time student or did you also work while you were in university?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I started as a full-time student, but later on I worked. I worked in Prnjavor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you attended schools, did you attend schools with non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were non-Serbs at the university. There were non-Serbs in my high school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while attending Banja Luka University, did you have non-Serb professors?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: As I was studying for my associate degree, I had more non-Serbian professors than Serbian professors, whereas at the university, the ratio was 50/50 when it came to non-Serbian and Serbian teachers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us you graduated with your university degree in 1980. And became a police officer in 1990. I'd like for you to describe briefly to the Chamber what you did in the ten years between 1980 and 1990. What municipality did you work in first of all?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Between -- I started working in 1975 as an inspector. That was a market inspector. Later on, I was an official in the local government. I was the secretary for economy and finances. I was the head of that department, that is. Then I was the director of a tax administration, the vice-president of the executive council, the executive board, of Prnjavor Municipality. And then on the 1st of April 1990, I was appointed the head of the public security station in Prnjavor, the chief of police in Prnjavor. So that would be my career in short.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you prior to assuming the position as the head of the public security station in Prnjavor, did you work as a reserve police officer as well?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After my compulsory military service in 1975, until the moment I was appointed the chief of the police, I was a member of the reserve police of the public security station in Prnjavor. I attended certain courses. I underwent certain training as a reserve policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to 1990, were you ever a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, that is, of the communist party of Yugoslavia if you want me to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of a socialist party?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the socialist party from 1994, and that would be my entire political engagement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So obviously you were never a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I was never an SDS member. And I wouldn't be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that in 1990, you were appointed the head of the public security station. What qualified you to assume that position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: In order to become the chief of police in Prnjavor, according to the regulations that were in effect in the ex-Yugoslavia, that is, in the then Bosnia and Herzegovina, I had to meet the following criteria: I had to have a full university degree. One of the four. I had to have a degree in law, in economics, security and safety, or any other humanities. I had to have certain work experience. Within that work experience, three years in managerial position. And I was supposed to have a bar exam -- not a bar exam, a state exam which qualified me to work in a state institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it required that you have any experience in administering or heading up a governmental agency?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the head of one of the organs of the executive council of Prnjavor Municipality. I was the secretary for economy there. And that was one of the things that qualified me for this position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who proposed you for this position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was proposed by municipal bodies. Proposals came from the executive council, that is, from the executive board, from the municipal assembly. So that's where the proposals came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who ultimately appointed you to your position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: The procedure was as follows: Once it was established that I met all the criteria, I was nominated by the executive board of the municipal assembly, and I was then appointed by the then minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe that his name was Besic. In any case, it was the minister who -- in whose purview it was to appoint me to become the chief of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991 -- from 1990 through the end of 1992, obviously you were originally assigned in Prnjavor. Did you get relocated to another municipality during 1990 through 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Between 1990 and 1992, I was the chief of police in Prnjavor. From the end of April 1992 to the end of March 1998, I was relocated to the public security centre in Banja Luka. And there I occupied several different positions. During that period of six years, I worked in several municipalities in the territory of Banja Luka, and I would spend anything between three days to three months working in those different municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Focussing in on 1992 after you were transferred to Banja Luka, did the nature of your job with the police, did it take you to municipalities -- other municipalities during that time period, the rest of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the -- in 1990 when you took over as chief of police in Prnjavor, what was the ethnic makeup, roughly speaking, of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: The municipality had about 50.000 inhabitants. About 13 to 14 per cent were Muslims. About 4 per cent were Croats. About 72 per cent were Serbs. And there were also other nationalities like Ukrainians and so on and so forth. In Prnjavor municipality at that time, there were 17 different ethnic groups residing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like for you to tell the Chamber about the hierarchy within the police in Bosnia-Herzegovina as it existed in 1991 and 1992. If we were to look at this hierarchy, who would be at the very top of the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: At the very top of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina was a minister. Minister was a member of the government of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the then Bosnia and Herzegovina. He had his assistants. Those were assistants for different segments within the Ministry of the Interior. So there were people who were in charge of the uniformed police. There was a person who was in charge of the crime prevention. The person who was in charge for national security. A person in charge of general administration, for finances and so on and so forth. So that was the second echelon of people next to the minister. Coming down the ladder, there were other people. The first amongst them was chiefs of security services centres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there. Where were the security service centres located at, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: The SBs mostly covered the regions of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So there was a CSB in Mostar, a CSB Sarajevo, a CSB Zenica, CSB Tuzla, CSB Doboj, CSB Banja Luka, and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I may have omitted one or two, but that was basically the structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So which centre was Prnjavor affiliated with?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: The public security station in Prnjavor was affiliated with Banja Luka. Gradiska was also one of those public security stations affiliated with Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the head or the chief of the centre called? Did he have a specific title?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: The chief of CSB Banja Luka. That was the title. And then there was me, the chief of public security station in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if the minister of the interior or any of his deputies gave you an order, were you obligated to follow it in 1990, 1991, and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Minister was at the head of that organ and whatever orders he issued we had to follow, providing those orders were in keeping with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the same apply to the chiefs that were at the level below the minister and his deputy ministers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The same applied to the chief of CSB, also providing that his orders were in keeping with the law and our internal regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If the minister or any of his deputy ministers gave a police officer an order and that order was not carried out, could that police officer be punished? Could he face a sanction for not carrying out the order of a superior?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is regulated by the law and by our internal regulations and should a subordinate refuse to carry out an order, he would be disciplined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the law that you're talking about, is that the law on internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the law on internal affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later on of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During 1991 and 1992, did the president of the municipality or the president of a municipal crisis staff have the authority to issue a direct order to a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, no, no, I don't think he did, because we operated exclusively according to our own legal provisions and legal documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a -- did presidents -- was it common for the president of the municipality or of a crisis staff to make a request of the CSB?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you about the CSB, but I can tell you about the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was it common in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't common in 1991 and 1992 as regards the public security station in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were the head of the public security station in Prnjavor, did the president of the municipality ever try to order you to do a specific act?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: The president of the municipality was -- while I was the chief of the public security station in Prnjavor could never issue an order to me. That's how it was due to circumstances. There were talks and agreements about certain ordinary matters, trivial matters, so to speak. For example, escorting cargo, securing a rally, something of that sort. And this was all regulated in our legal provisions. It's true that he never issued an order to me, nor did he ever ask me to do anything unusual. Had he done so, I would not have complied because I had very strict instructions from the chief of the centre and the ministry. And those orders were that I was to work in accordance with our legal provisions and our regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the chief of the centre who gave you the order that you were to work within the legal provisions and regulations? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: At that time it was Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, I've got the exhibits in the binder if Serbian if they can be tendered to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, if you look in that exhibit book what you'll see are red tabs on the right-hand side of the paper, and you'll see numbers on the tabs. When I direct you to a specific document, what I'd like for you to do is go through that document. I left many of these documents with you last night, and I don't think I left the first one with you, which is P25. In a minute I'm going to have you look at that document, but I want to ask you some questions first. In the multiparty elections with Prnjavor being a predominantly Serb municipality, which political party won the elections?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: At the multiparty elections of 1990, it was the Serbian Democratic Party that won the majority of votes, and therefore the largest number of seats in the municipal assembly and higher up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the president of the municipality, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: His name was Nemanja Vasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in the Prnjavor, did the SDA still participate in the government? Were they still participating?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: The SDA were participating in the municipal government. And as far as I can recall, they had seven or nine assemblymen in the local assembly. I can't remember the exact number. And they also had two officials in the executive board of the municipal assembly. That is, in the executive branch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the HDZ? Were they participating in the government, municipal government, when you left Prnjavor, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: There were few Croats, only about 4 per cent. And they were mostly in the villages of Kulasi, Drenova, Babanovci, so the HDZ was not formally organised in the Prnjavor Municipality, although it was active.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The first document I'm going to want you to look at is the very first document there. It should have tab number 25 on it. That is a document that was dated 19 December 1991 by the SDS main board in Sarajevo. And this document is called: "Instructions for the organisation and activities of the organs of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina under extraordinary circumstances."

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman tells me we need to have the technicians turn on the Sanction programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did the technicians -- Mr. Ackerman is suggesting that he can't use the Sanction until and unless it's switched on. Can I have a feedback from the technicians, please, at least letting me know if there is a problem. Which document is this in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It's P25, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I don't want to waste time in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I've got copies available, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you find P25 in English, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Madam usher, the first page I'm going to use is the one that has paragraph 3 on it, and I think it's already highlighted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a word from the technicians, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: She is calling someone else to come to the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the English version on the ELMO, please. Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think it's already highlighted on...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I noticed while we were dealing with the technical questions, sir, that you were looking through the document. My first question to you is have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I have never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in Prnjavor, did you ever hear any of the Serbs in municipal government or any of the Serbs in that municipality discussing this document and variant A and variant B and the contents of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. As I was not a member of the executive board of the municipal assembly, I was not able to get hold of this plan. This is the first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 3, which should be in front of you, it's on the first page, says that -- paragraph 3 says that the SDS municipal board will immediately form a crisis staff of the Serbian people. And if you look under the list of people underneath there, it says the chief of the public security station or commander of the police station should be a member of the crisis staff. Were you ever a member of a crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I was never a member of a crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 6 in that same document, paragraph 6 talks about increasing security of critical facilities within the municipality. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Is it here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're looking for paragraph 6 on Exhibit 25.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Can you say what page it's on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have the... It should either be on the very first page or the second page of the text. If you don't see it there, let me just go ahead and put the question to you, because in our English version it clearly shows up. And paragraph number 6 says this, sir. It says: "Increase security of critical facilities within the municipality." You've found it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've found it now, yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just reassured myself that I'm not going crazy. Paragraph number 6, was -- in the first two or three months of the year 1991, was there a feeling that war was approaching?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was a feeling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you and the other police officers take steps to protect critical facilities within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: We took steps, and we had a task to secure crucial facilities. This was an ongoing task. And this refers to electrical power lines, important bridges, telephone and telegraph communications, roads, railways, and also we stepped up security measures in villages that were of a multiethnic composition, especially the village of Lisuja and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you take steps to ensure increased security for the non-Serbian areas?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: We were afraid of interethnic problems and clashes. And we had an ongoing task to make the security situation as good and secure as possible after the multiparty elections and to protect those communities because there were members of minority populations, non-Serb populations, on the territory of Prnjavor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you establish mixed patrols, mixed ethnicities patrolling in these areas?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: In all the villages where there were non-Serb inhabitants, we formed exclusively mixed patrols. I won't go into a detailed list of these villages. But under my orders, it was only mixed patrols that were established comprising Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and members of other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have requests from the leaders of the non-Serbian community to provide increased police presence in their villages or hamlets?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was especially evident in the Party of Democratic Action. Mr. Husein Vukovic who was the president of the SDA in Prnjavor. Also, some people who were Croats from Dragalovici and Kulasi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Look at -- and it appears that Sanction is now working, Your Honours. Look at paragraph number 11. It's going to be in that same document, sir. Paragraph number 11 talks about carrying out specific preparations for the protection of, and you'll see a list of four or five things there. Take the time and read that to yourself. With respect to paragraph number 11, did anyone either at the centre in Banja Luka or any of your superiors ever give you this order to carry out these preparations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: This particular order? No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If we go further down in this document, sir, you'll see that it starts talking about -- there's a heading that says the second stage of variant A. And in paragraph 2, there is a following quote. It says: "Mobilise all police forces from the ranks of the Serbian people. And in cooperation with the command posts and headquarters of the JNA, ensure their gradual subordination." Do you see that paragraph in your copy?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive an order from anyone with respect to this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: No, we had a completely different system of work. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at that paragraph, it says: "Mobilise all police forces from the ranks of the Serbian people." That suggests at least to me that the police officers should all be members of the Serb ethnic group. During the time that you were in Prnjavor, were there Serbs -- were there non-Serbs under your direct command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Whenever I was chief of police in Prnjavor, I had both active-duty and reserve policemen belonging to other ethnic groups in proportion to the ethnic makeup of the population of the Municipality of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you left Prnjavor on 1 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you left 1 April 1992, were there still non-Serbs under your command in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: When I left Prnjavor on the 2nd of April 1992, part of the non-Serb policemen had left their work in the police station. I was aware of that. But there was still a number of non-Serb policemen who remained working in Prnjavor police station after my departure. This included Muslims, Croats, Ukrainians, and they are still working in the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did the -- you said that some non-Serbian police officers left. Do you know why they left?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Well, why did they leave? Some left because the uniforms and insignia were changed. Some left because the composition of the police force was not the same as it had been, and others left for economic reasons. They saw what was coming. And some left because they were fired. They were dismissed. So there were several reasons, not just one, why they left the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take the second-to-the last one talked about. The economic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reasons You said that they saw what was coming. Can you explain what you meant about that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: People realised that there was going to be a war, that there would be enormous problems, both political and economic. They lacked the means to live more and more. More and more people were left without work. And they thought of leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina and going to a western country. There were many such cases in Prnjavor Municipality and elsewhere, but it's well known that almost a third of the population of Prnjavor are migrant workers either temporarily or permanently employed in western Europe. So people had relatives working in Sweden, Germany. Most of them went to Sweden. Some went to Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Serbs leaving because of these same economic reasons you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite a lot of Serbs left for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your answer you also said that some left because they were fired, they were dismissed. Why were they fired? Why were they dismissed? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: In my time, there were policemen from the territory of Croatia and other republics, such as Slovenia. They came from there, and we employed them. They were Serbs who had been dismissed in Croatia or Slovenia for ethnic reasons. And this probably happened after the 1st of April in our area, that some policemen were dismissed because they were not Serbs. This was a system of cause and effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by cause and effect, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Well, at least to my mind, as many Serbs had arrived from Croatia and been accepted in the ranks of the police force, the then authorities then carried out tit for tat dismissals, so that many non-Serbs stopped working in the police in 1992. I think this was a response to the authorities in Croatia, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and other parts of former Yugoslavia where there were interethnic problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to have you tell the Chamber briefly about the police work that was done by you and your police officers before you left. Specifically I'd like to know, was there any distinction drawn within your police force about -- between Serbs and non-Serbs? Were they treated differently?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. What time period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time, let's say, from the last six months of your stay in Prnjavor, which would mean the last three months of 1990 and the first three months of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand now. Until the 1st of April 1992, non-Serb policemen had all the rights and enjoyed exactly the same rights as Serbs in the public security station. I in the leadership of the police station did not permit any sort of interethnic tensions. And while I was the chief of police up to the 1st of April, none of the non-Serbs were dismissed. They were all deployed, and they all enjoyed the same treatment as Serb policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to those police officers under your command, how did they work in the field? Were they -- did they treat all the ethnic groups the same? Did they do their jobs professionally? How would you characterise the police officers under your command, during that same time period, last three months of 1991 through 1992? First three months of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I can state responsibly that the policemen acted fully professionally. There were patrols composed of mixed ethnicity, and they worked on the territory of the entire municipality. This refers to both the active-duty and the reserve policemen under my command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, before we continue, we need to correct this. And I thank Judge Taya for attracting my attention to this. Page 22, lines 13 and 14, 1990 and 1991 should read 1991 and 1992 respectively. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to change topics on you now, and I'm done with Exhibit Number 25. Who was the chief of the centre in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: It was Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the last three or four months of 1991 and the first three or four months of 1992 while you were still the chief of police in Prnjavor, did you have meetings with Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had meetings with him. They were regular weekly meetings. And it was not just me who attended those meetings, but also other chiefs from the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at these weekly meetings, on the average how many chiefs or their representatives would be at these meetings with Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: It depended on the situation and on the specific things that were to be discussed. If we were discussing crimes, then it would be heads of crime departments. If it was public order, then it would be chiefs of police. So it all depended on the situation and on the issues that were discussed at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these meetings while you were the chief of police in Prnjavor, did the subject of paramilitary groups ever come up?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the most usual topic, and it was on the agenda of every -- almost every meeting. Throughout 1991, throughout 1992, and the beginning of 1993, that was a very common topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you discuss the disarming of Serb paramilitaries -- excuse me, the disarming of paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which paramilitary groups, what ethnicity was the primary focus of these meetings if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: We mostly discussed Serb paramilitaries, but we also discussed other paramilitaries composed of other ethnic groups but which were not within the scope of our municipality. We mostly discussed those that were in our territory, and we discussed what to do with them. That was my biggest problem, my most pronounced problem at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the binder on the desk, I want you to look at red tab that has number 82 on it. And let me know when you have located that document.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a letter signed by the chief of the centre, Stojan Zupljanin, directed to a number of different entities, discussing, does it not, the problems of armed groups within the territory covered by the centre?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you talked about discussion of the problem of armed Serbian paramilitaries within the region, is this document indicative of the centre's concern for these paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is not just an indication. This is what really happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the paramilitaries was Veljko Milankovic's group, one of the groups of paramilitaries operating within this area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a subject of concern?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and other chiefs receive direct orders from the chief of the centre to take down and arrest Veljko Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was Milankovic a concern to public security?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Veljko Milankovic's paramilitary were active in Prnjavor. They threatened peace and order and security in the municipality. They caused problems. They caused trouble. Not only in Prnjavor, but also in the general region of Prnjavor. And that resulted in some problems. I wanted him disarmed or placed under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army. At those meetings, we discussed how to disarm him and neutralise his activities in the municipality of Prnjavor and in the general area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say something interesting when you say "I wanted him disarmed or placed under the command of the JNA." What was the thinking with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. respect to placing him under the command of the JNA? The reason I bring that up, it seems odd because on hand you call him a criminal, and on the other hand you want him under the control of the JNA. What was the rationale or the thinking --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: When I say under the control of the JNA, this would mean that all his members would be disarmed and incorporated within regular units, not as the entire unit but every individual according to his specialty should have been put in various units of the JNA. In simple words, this paramilitary unit should have been disbanded and put under the control of the JNA. They were all military conscripts in any case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, were you involved in arresting Mr. Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: It happened in mid-October 1992 or in late October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by this time, you had left Prnjavor and gone to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Not 1992. I apologise. It was in 1991. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Where was he arrested at, in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the territory of Prnjavor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber how his arrest came about.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: There were problems, and I informed of these problems the chief of public security of Banja Luka every day. At one of the meetings the plans were made to disarm Veljko Milankovic's group. I conducted an operation with assistance of policeman who had arrived from the CSB. They came to assist us in Prnjavor. The group was disarmed. Veljko and his aides were arrested. Their weapons were seized and handed over to the JNA. Criminal reports or various criminal reports were filed against Veljko for various criminal acts that he had committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was taken into custody, and he was remanded for about a month, for over 20 days in any case. I don't remember exactly how long he was in custody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time how many men were in his group?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: At that time, there were about 60 or so men in his group. They started with 21 men, and then their size increased to 60. Their number varied, but at that time there were about 60 people in his group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when Veljko was arrested, were any of his men arrested with him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two or three others were taken into custody. They were soon released, but he remained in prison. They were all taken into custody, and then after the initial interviews, they were all released. There was screening, after which they were released, and he was taken to the CSB in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the arrest of Veljko taken as a direct result of the order of the director of the centre in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the order came from Banja Luka upon my insistence I think it's fair to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform Mr. Zupljanin about Mr. Milankovic's arrest?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Stojan was directly involved. I only informed him when Veljko was actually taken into custody, when he was apprehended. He was up to speed about the events all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you mean when you say he was directly involved?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he planned the whole operation with me, the plans were drawn on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that Milankovic was released after 20 days, 3 weeks, something like that. What was your reaction when you found out this man you had arrested, insisted on being arrested, was released?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I learned that around midnight from my employees. I didn't know previously that he would be released. All of us in the public security station were shocked. We were embittered when we learned that he had been released because we knew that we would again have problems with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever call Stojan Zupljanin in Banja Luka to find out what had happened? Talk to him about the release?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I called the chief of police. He was also surprised and angry. And he told me "I really don't know what to do. I don't know how to go on from here."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that there was -- and I think it was your thoughts, that he could be controlled if he was placed under the control of the army. Do you know whether or not that ever happened?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Later on he was placed under control of the 1st Krajina Corps, together with his unit. What was the form of that control, I don't know, but I know that after I left he had been placed under the control of the then JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that binder in front of you, sir, there is an exhibit tabbed 400. If you look on page 5 -- and let me identify this for the record. This is in evidence. It is a 28 July 1992 report on paramilitary formations in the territory of the Serbian Republic of BiH. It is -- at the top appears the BH Army main staff department of intelligence and security affairs. If we look at page 5, we see the following: "The detachment of Veljko Milankovic from Prnjavor has 150 men and is, as of recently, formally under the command of the 1st KK. Members of this detachment are involved in extensive looting and recently attacked the Tactical Group 3 Command Post, arresting one SRBH Army colonel in the process." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he wasn't arrested and kept in jail rather than incorporating him into the army?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Here, a group of 150 men are mentioned. He had less men than that, so I don't know where this number comes from. Why he was put under the command of the 1st KK, I don't know. But I remember having insisted of him being placed under the command of the JNA. But even after that, he continued his usual practices; that is, his group continued whatever they were doing before that. And why the measures were not taken at the time in keeping with the law on the army, I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that Milankovic was a topic of the meetings, the weekly meetings that you attended with the chief of the centre in Banja Luka. Let me ask you this: At those meetings that you attended, was there ever any discussion planning for Serb police officers to expel non-Serbian members of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: No, not at those meetings, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking back at those meetings, was there ever anything other than legitimate police work or security concerns discussed at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: At those meetings, nothing. Now, whether there were things discussed elsewhere, I don't know. At those meetings that I attended, we discussed nothing but the regular police work, and the regular police work at that time was difficult enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm assuming that you also had contact with Stojan Zupljanin over the phone during this time period. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these telephone conversations, were there any discussions planning of the Serbs to take over the Krajina and expel the non-Serbian population? Was that ever broached in any private conversation that you had with the chief of the centre in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I don't think so. However, the general situation was such that one could sense it in the air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sense what in the air?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: There was the war psychosis. There was war in Croatia. There were paramilitaries, the Green Berets, the HOS. We were on this side here. There were several municipalities which were blocked. The Serbian population in those municipalities was encircled. So the situation had already come to a head, and we were just waiting for things to explode.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that your final day as the chief of police in Prnjavor was 1 April 1992. Do you know why -- what happened with your job?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of April, I was told that I would be replaced by Vincic Radislav, and I was told that I would no longer be chief and that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. other heads of department would no longer be heads of department, that from then on we would be required to take the leave of absence and that our further engagement would be decided on by Stojan Zupljanin. Obviously there were some complaints. However, we understood what the situation was, and we decided to take this decision and leave our jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you the news? Who told you that you were being replaced?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the previous two or three days, Stojan Zupljanin indicated to me that I would no longer be chief, and I was told directly by the newly appointed chief of police, Radoslav Vincic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you given a reason why you were being replaced?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: No. No reasons were given. But I assumed -- I knew why I was being replaced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: In political terms, I did not fit, and I did not meet requirements. I was not an SDS member. I was against the war. And I was against the new organisation of the police in terms of its ethnic composition and in terms of its organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Cunningham. As a policeman or as a member of the police corps, could you belong to a political party, or was it prohibited at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, it was not prohibited. You could belong to a party. And not only that you could, but it was one of the requirements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talk about the new organisation of the police in terms of its ethnic composition, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I believe then, and I still believe, that the police should reflect the ethnic composition of the municipality where it is active, regardless of the fact that the municipality is in the Republika Srpska under the Serbian government. So it was my belief that the police should also have non-Serb members in proportion to the ethnic composition of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that changing or about to change when you left?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: After I left, things started changing in the public security station in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And going back to what we talked about earlier, your next job in Banja Luka, did it take you to Prnjavor during the rest of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And although --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And although the ethnic composition of the police force had started to change in -- after you left, were there still non-Serbs working within the police force when you would go there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and some of them have stayed until this very day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also talked about how you were against the new organisation of the police in terms of its very organisation. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I believed that people working in the police should be professionals rather than politically fit. And people who started joining the police at that time were people who were politically correct, and I was against that. I wanted only professionals to work in the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were transferred to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your job title in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I was an inspector for the white-collar crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And who -- were you still under the control of the director in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was under direct control of the CSB, its department for the white-collar crime. The head of the CSB at the time was still Stojan Zupljanin, but he was not my direct superior. I did not report to him directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And briefly tell us what the new duties in this new position involved?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: My new duties fell under the area of the white-colour crime, money laundering, smuggling, tax evasion, abuse of position in economy and in services. So I had a wide range of duties and tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Banja Luka? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I arrived in Banja Luka on the 20th of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it you were not present when the SOS arrived in Banja Luka in early April? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: That is true. I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to go into a new area if this is a good place to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Savic, we are going to have a 25-minute break, which basically means we will reconvene at roughly 10 to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we left off, I was about to talk to you about the conditions in Banja Luka. From your arrival, the second half of April 1992, until the end of 1992, you told us in the context of your job as a white-collar crime investigator for the centre that you travelled extensively throughout the region in 1992. I want you to think about the places that you went to in 1992, and compare that to Banja Luka in 1992. How would you rate Banja Luka in terms of safety for its inhabitants as compared to those other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your microphone wasn't on, so start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: As an inspector, I visited almost all the municipalities in the area and further afield, and I spent the most time in Grahovo, Petrovic, Kljuc, Prnjavor you know about. Gradiska, Laktasi, and other municipalities. These municipalities, with the exception of Gradiska, in this part were affected by the war. And going out into the field, I can say that I was happiest when I was returning to Banja Luka where I had temporary accommodation. And this was because Banja Luka for me and for most of the population was one of the safest towns, unlike Mrkonjic and Sipovo where we also arrested criminals and disarmed them. Banja Luka in my view was naturally the safest town at the time. And Banja Luka now has over 200.000 inhabitants. At that time, it was one of the centres of the then Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I felt far safer there than I did in my native Prnjavor. I'm saying this because there were fewer uniformed soldiers there. There were fewer incidents. They were rare in Banja Luka, unlike other places such as Sipovo, Mrkonjic, or Prnjavor. In Banja Luka, there were no paramilitary troops [Realtime transcript read in error "there were paramilitary troops"], and this was another reason why it was a safer town than others. That's why I feel that Banja Luka was a relatively good place to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that there were no problems in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it doesn't mean that there were no problems at all. But they were not as bad as in other places as regards security. I'm only speaking in terms of security. There were incidents, but they were marginal and minor in comparison to Sipovo or Bosanski Petrovac, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The crimes that you were investigating in Banja Luka and the other municipalities, were you only investigating non-Serbs? Were non-Serbs only being charged in your investigations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I wasn't investigating those kind of crimes, but only economic and other white-collar crimes. And for the most part, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. investigated Serbs. I think there was only one Muslim against whom I filed a criminal report. For the most part, they were all Serbs. It was mostly Serbs who committed those kind of crimes that I was in charge of. So as far as I was concerned, the non-Serbs were not investigated, but I know that all criminals were investigated in the police overall. And I know that measures were taken against both Serbs and members of other ethnic groups who committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've got an error in the transcript. LiveNote page 35, line 13. It reflects that he says that there were paramilitaries, paramilitary troops in Banja Luka. He said that there were no paramilitary troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There were no, no. That's what I heard anyway. Thank you, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to -- did you have contact with police officers who were assigned to investigate cases within Banja Luka Municipality itself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, due to circumstances we did have contact. And of course, there were policemen who took certain measures against those who stole people's cars, broke into their flats. They were armed people. There was mistreatment and so on. I remember some details, some I probably don't. But I know that this was a regular task of the security services in the Republika Srpska, in the then Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Banja Luka. Policemen did their jobs professionally, and also policemen in my line of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Getting back to the question I asked you about Banja Luka, based on your conversations and your observations, conversations with and your observations of officers working in the Banja Luka Municipality, were they neglecting the complaints of the non-Serbian population? Were they treating the non-Serb population differently?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: In my department, it was all fully professional. There was no neglect. I know that in other departments, they also acted on complaints. Maybe they didn't always, but I can state and affirm that in my department we acted on every complaint. Our chief insisted on giving priority to non-Serbs. That was my direct superior, to non-Serbs who filed complaints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if other departments followed the same approach that your department did?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Well, some departments did. I gleaned that from private conversations with my colleagues from other departments. There were also non-Serbs employed in the centre among the inspectors and other employees so that what I knew I knew mainly from private conversations. In my department, this was a priority. My superior always gave priority to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to follow up on something you just said, that there were also non-Serbs employed in the centre. Was that throughout 1992, that there were non-Serb investigators and officers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I can give you their names, those who are still employed there. There were Muslims, there were Croats working with me, Ukrainians, and members of other ethnic groups, and I can even tell you their names. Their first and last names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think that's necessary. You told us earlier while you attended school in Banja Luka, your secondary school and your preuniversity studies, and your university studies that you had non-Serbian friends and non-Serbian professors. During 1992 did you have the opportunity to speak with your former colleagues from your student days?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I still have these friends, and I had them during the war. Some left. Some stayed behind. But we kept in touch. I kept in touch with my colleagues and my teachers, my professors, who were non-Serbs, and I can give you their names, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how, if at all, the war was affecting them or how the life in Banja Luka in 1992 was affecting them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: My views and theirs differed very little. When we exchanged opinions, we had the same standpoint about the war, about what was happening in Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, about the reasons for the interethnic tensions and conflicts. We all thought that we were worse off than before. Some left. Some for economic reasons; others for security reasons. Some also, of course, had problems. And we all thought, in fact, that things had gone from bad to worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Banja Luka working in these various municipalities doing white-collar crime investigations, did you ever hear discussions, conversations about the red combi that was used to seize people and the subject of many complaints? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, 1996, I think it was in 1996 that I heard about a van, a combi, but not a red one, a yellow one. I only heard about this after the war in 1996. In some conversations among policemen, there was a red or a yellow combi van that was mentioned. But I heard this only after the war, not during the war when certain investigations were starting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The investigation of what I'll call street crime, violent street crime, was that within your realm of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: As for street crime, that's a broad concept. But if you're referring to black marketeering, then it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I tried to cross cultures and give you an American's definition of street crime. When I talk about street crime, I'm talking about robbery, burglary, car theft. Things of that nature. Was that within your realm of responsibility when you were in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, in part, especially taking vehicles away from people, both Serbs and non-Serbs, taking goods away from people. That fell within my purview, and this is where we took measures and filed criminal reports in every such case. But this only had to do with goods, money, cars, and such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now while you were in Banja Luka during April through the end of 1992, did you become aware of an entity known as the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew it existed. It was not a secret. It was published in the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in -- I want you to go back to the notebook that's in front of you and look for the red tab marked 202, because we're going to talk about Exhibit 202. Once you find it, I'm going to direct your attention to paragraph 23. I think it has been highlighted for you in yellow highlights. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document dated 20 May from the Banja Luka security service centre conclusions dating back to 6 May 1992. And it's signed by -- attributed to the chief of the centre, Stojan Zupljanin. I want you to look at paragraph number 23 and read that to yourself. That paragraphs says: "In all our activities, we are obliged to observe all measures and to apply all procedures ordered by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region." First of all, did you ever see this order, physically see it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: No. If I had been the chief of police at the time, I would probably have seen it because it would have arrived by dispatch. But as things were, no, I never saw it physically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did your supervisor ever talk with you about paragraph number 23?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the department I worked in?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was there ever any discussion among you and the other investigators about having to abide by this paragraph number 23?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: There were informal conversations, but professionally speaking all policemen trained in that time, we all adhered to the commands issued by our superiors and the minister. I see this was in May 1992, but there are instructions dating from 1991 -- yes, 1991, where Stojan Zupljanin says the opposite of this, where he orders us to obey exclusively orders coming from him and the minister, not from municipal authorities. Then there Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were no crisis staffs. We were not to obey crisis staffs or other civil bodies. So there was a dispatch where we were told to adhere to instructions and orders from the minister, or rather the chief of the public security centre or other people authorised by them. I am now speaking of 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this order, you know from looking at it, it dates from 6 May 1992. Was that directive in paragraph 23 -- as far as you know, was that ever implemented by you or any other member of the police force?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Whether it was implemented, I couldn't say because it depended on the chief of police in each particular municipality. I can say that I would not accept this unless I received written instructions to that effect from my superior or from the minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if -- you told us how in 1990 and 1991 there were orders to the contrary; that is, you only obey the minister or the chief of the security centre. Do you know after the date of this document, which is -- it's in May of 1992, whether there were orders, directives, that went back to what was the procedure in 1991 and 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I think this was written just as a matter of form. We obeyed the chief of the security service centres and the minister. I think this is something that was simply put there. We did the same -- we operated in the same way we had before. It was -- the orders we received always came from our superiors, and I'm referring now to uniformed policemen. They received instructions from their superiors, not the crisis staff. And this was not mentioned. This is a very specific area, and I know that we worked only under instructions coming from Stojan or from the ministry. We had our own organisation, just as every other police force has, and this was simply something that was put on paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to change topics on you now. And I want you to look in that book at Exhibit P388. It should be on the tab. Because I'm going to talk to you about Teslic and the Mice.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, did you receive -- were you tasked to go to Teslic to deal with a problem in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the problem that the municipal authorities in Teslic were having?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 28th of June 1992, or maybe the 27th of June 1992. A few of us, including Predrag Radulovic, known as Pile, myself, Dusan Kos, and some other inspectors were summoned to Stojan Zupljanin's office. He dictated a task to us, or rather he gave us our instructions orally. And then he said to Predrag -- should I go on? He said to Predrag that we should go to Teslic. Predrag knew about this already. And he said: "Well, I've given you Milenko as well. He has experience with paramilitaries and organising a station."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there. What was the problem in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: The problem in Teslic was, at least what I heard about it at the meeting, that there was a paramilitary unit similar to something that had happened in Prnjavor in 1991. That is, there were paramilitaries acting illegally on the ground, confiscating weapons, goods, driving people out of their houses, robbing them, stealing money and so on. And I understood that the situation was similar but far worse than had been the case in Prnjavor because in Prnjavor there were policemen around who were more efficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Mice in Teslic, did they differentiate between the non-Serb and the Serbian population when they would commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: In part, maybe they did. But there were also Serbs, wealthy Serbs, who had been robbed, and the Serbs suffered quite a lot, too. There were also confiscations of vehicles from Serbs, robberies, mistreatment, and so on. So that the army also at one point objected to the activities of that paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where were the police -- why couldn't they deal with the Mice in Teslic? You said earlier that they were -- in Prnjavor, you had policemen who were more efficient. What was the problem with the police force in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: When these paramilitaries who had arrived from Doboj, and there was a large number of them, when they arrived in Teslic, the first thing they did was to put the police under their total control. The chief of police, they practically drove him away from the station. The commander as well. And the police had to obey their orders or they would have problems involving firearms. The police did complain, but there was nothing they could do. That's why the police could not act efficiently for the month and a half or two while these people were in Doboj. A similar situation could have occurred in Prnjavor, but we prevented it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what specific task did you and Mr. Radulovic and others get from Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Predrag Radulovic was the chief of police. Dusan Kos was the police commander. I was the chief of the criminal investigations police in Teslic. And we went to Teslic with this task. Our chief objective was to disarm the paramilitary unit to document what had happened and to file criminal reports with a competent court. That was our main objective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in your answer, you say: Mr. Radulovic was the chief of police, Mr. Kos was the police commander, and you were the chief of the criminal investigation police. Are those designations --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They're designations you received from the director of the centre. Correct?
